title: Periodontal Phenotype Modification of Mandibular Incisors Following Augmented Corticotomy During Orthodontic–Orthognathic Treatment in Skeletal Class III Patients: A Long‐Term Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To prospectively evaluate periodontal soft‐ and hard‐tissue changes in the mandibular incisor region after labial augmented corticotomy (AC) in skeletal Class III patients undergoing orthodontic–orthognathic treatment. Materials and Methods Thirty‐five skeletal Class III patients were included. A total of 140 mandibular incisors treated with AC were evaluated at baseline, 6 months after surgery and at treatment completion. Clinical parameters, gingival thickness, cemento‐enamel junction (CEJ) to alveolar crest distance and labial and lingual alveolar bone areas were assessed using clinical examination, cone‐beam computed tomography and integrated digital models. Results Probing depth and labial gingival recession showed no significant overall changes. Width of keratinised gingiva and gingival thickness increased significantly and remained higher than baseline at treatment completion. Labial CEJ to alveolar crest distance decreased and remained lower than baseline, whereas the lingual distance increased. Labial alveolar bone area remained higher than baseline, whereas lingual alveolar bone area progressively decreased over time. Conclusions Labial AC was associated with sustained improvement in periodontal soft tissue and labial alveolar bone in the mandibular incisor region through treatment completion, although lingual alveolar bone area decreased over time.

title: A Split‐Mouth Randomised Controlled Clinical Trial: Comparing Ostectomy Performed With Piezosurgery Versus Burs for Aesthetic Crown‐Lengthening Surgery
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To assess the clinical, profilometric, radiographic and patient‐reported outcomes following aesthetic crown lengthening (ECL) with ostectomy performed using either piezosurgery (PS) or rotary burs (RB). Methods Fifteen patients with altered passive eruption underwent ECL from maxillary premolar to premolar in a 6‐month split‐mouth randomised design. Ostectomy was performed with either PS or RB. Clinical, profilometric and radiographic assessments, as well as patient‐reported outcomes, were collected. The primary outcome was the change in gingival margin (GM) position between 6 weeks and 6 months, analysed with a linear mixed model with treatment as a fixed effect and patient as a random effect. Results Between 6 weeks and 6 months (primary outcome), GM change was 0.16 ± 0.19 mm in the PS group and 0.12 ± 0.21 mm in the RB group ( p = 0.170). The greatest reduction in crown height occurred between suturing and 7 days (−0.63 ± 0.35 mm). CEJ–BC remodelling from surgery to 6 months was −0.22 ± 0.42 mm ( PS ) and −0.26 ± 0.44 mm ( RB ) ( p = 0.491). Conclusion PS and RB showed no significant difference in GM stability following ECL, with the greatest changes in the first week and stability by 6 weeks.

title: Immediate Implants With or Without a Volume Stable Collagen Matrix: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim This randomized clinical trial evaluated soft tissue thickness (STT) around immediate implants with or without soft tissue augmentation using a volume‐stable collagen matrix (VCMX). Secondary outcomes included clinical, esthetic, volumetric, and patient‐reported outcomes. Materials and Methods Participants received immediate implants in the anterior esthetic zone with (Test) or without (Control) simultaneous VCMX augmentation. Outcomes were assessed before surgery, immediately after surgery, and at 6 and 12 months. The primary outcome was STT. Within‐ and between‐group comparisons were performed using the Friedman rank test and Mann–Whitney U test, respectively. Secondary outcomes included mucosal level (ML), marginal bone level (MBL), esthetic and patient‐reported outcomes, and volumetric changes. Results Thirty‐eight out of 40 patients completed the study. STT was significantly greater in the Test group at all follow‐ups ( p p p = 0.0917), whereas STT in the Control group decreased non‐significantly at 3 mm (0.18 mm, SE 0.18, p = 0.6213) and at 6 mm (0.36 mm, SE 0.10, p = 0.1054). ML remained stable in the Test group but showed significant recession in the Control group. Selected esthetic and patient‐reported outcomes favored the Test group. MBL did not change significantly over time in either group. Volumetric analysis showed no significant change over time in the Test group, whereas the Control group showed significant shrinkage ( p = 0.0201). Conclusions VCMX augmentation may improve soft tissue stability around immediate implants. Trial Registration The study protocol was registered on September 20, 2021 in the ClinicalTrials.gov database (registration number: NCT05081284)

title: Probe Accuracy and Agreement and Patient Preferences in Peri‐Implant Probing Depth Assessment: A Cross‐Sectional Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To record the accuracy and agreement of three types of probes (i.e., a common metal probe and two types of flexible probes) for peri‐implant probing depth (PD) assessment, including patient‐reported outcomes (PRO). Methods Fifty patients (85 implants) with an implant‐supported restoration were included. Peri‐implant PD was recorded with a metal, plastic, and electronic probe. Pain/discomfort and patient preference were registered. After removing the prosthetic restoration, the correct peri‐implant PD (cPD), the mucosal height (MH), and the PD measured from the implant level (iPD) were assessed. Results Good accuracy and agreement were noted for PD measurements with the metal and plastic probe. They differed in approximately 80% of the measurements by Conclusions While the electronic probe was unreliable, the metal and plastic probes were relatively accurate and comparable for assessing peri‐implant PD; the plastic probe caused less pain/discomfort. However, in approximately 1/5 of the measurements a ≥ 1.5 mm deviation from the correct value (cPD) may occur, and the accuracy of the metal probe appears negatively influenced by a thick peri‐implant mucosal phenotype. Trial Registration The protocol was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05332327)

title: DFDBA With or Without Platelet‐Rich Fibrin in Maxillary Sinus Augmentation: A Randomized Split‐Mouth Clinical Trial
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To compare histologic and histomorphometric outcomes after bilateral lateral maxillary sinus augmentation with demineralized freeze‐dried bone allograft (DFDBA) alone versus DFDBA combined with platelet‐rich fibrin (PRF), and to report 1‐year prosthetic follow‐up of the restored implants. Materials and Methods This randomized split‐mouth clinical trial included subjects requiring bilateral lateral maxillary sinus augmentation before implant placement. In each subject, one sinus was randomly assigned to DFDBA alone and the contralateral sinus to DFDBA combined with leukocyte‐ and platelet‐rich fibrin (L‐PRF) and injectable PRF (i‐PRF). Bone biopsy specimens were harvested at the clinically relevant 6‐month implant placement time point. The primary outcome was newly formed bone. Secondary histomorphometric outcomes were residual graft material, connective tissue, and fibrosis; inflammation and necrosis were assessed histologically. Clinical and radiographic prosthetic follow‐up was performed 1 year after definitive prosthetic loading. Paired comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed‐rank test. Results Of 24 enrolled subjects, 21 completed follow‐up and contributed 42 sinus sites to the paired analysis. Median newly formed bone was 48.72% (IQR, 33.33%–63.33%) on the PRF side and 45.76% (IQR, 37.14%–54.90%) on the non‐PRF side ( p = 0.5). Residual graft material was 6.74% versus 4.23% ( p = 0.2), connective tissue was 31.48% versus 36.92% ( p = 0.016), and fibrosis was 3.42% versus 2.56% ( p > 0.9). No inflammation or necrosis was observed. Following replacement of one implant that failed before prosthetic loading, all definitively restored implants remained functional during the 1‐year prosthetic follow‐up. Clinical and radiographic follow‐up was uneventful, and no biologic or prosthetic complications requiring intervention were observed. Conclusions Adding PRF to DFDBA did not significantly increase newly formed bone at the 6‐month implant placement time point. The lower connective tissue proportion on the PRF side may suggest altered tissue maturation; however, this secondary finding should be interpreted cautiously. Definitively restored implants showed 100% prosthetic survival during 1‐year follow‐up. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07348198; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07348198 . This clinical trial was not registered prior to participant recruitment and randomization.

title: Effect of Non-Splinting Techniques and Non-Calibrated Implant Scan Body Systems on the Accuracy of Complete-Arch Implant Scans: A Comparative Clinical Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of complete‐arch implant scans obtained using non‐splinting and non‐calibrated implant scan body (ISB) methods captured by an intraoral scanner (IOS) with 2 scanning patterns with and without artificial intelligence (AI)‐based tools. Materials and Methods A patient with an edentulous maxillary arch and 4 implants was enrolled. Four groups were established according to scanning technique evaluated: non‐splinting with PEEK or titanium ISBs, 2 non‐calibrated ISBs methods. For each technique, the maxillary arch was scanned using an IOS, applying both a circumferential and an occlusal‐buccal‐lingual scanning pattern, with and without the use of the integrated AI‐based tool of the selected IOS. A stone cast fabricated through the conventional splinted impression was verified and digitized with a laboratory scanner to serve as reference. Linear and angular discrepancies among the designed bars for reference and experimental scans were analyzed. Results Non‐calibrated techniques demonstrated better linear trueness and better angular trueness and precision than non‐splinting methods ( p p > 0.05). The titanium ISBs of the non‐splinting group resulted in better trueness and precision than the PEEK ISBs ( p p p > 0.05). Conclusions Implant scanning technique and AI‐based tool of the IOS selected influenced the accuracy of the complete‐arch implant scans; however, the scanning pattern did not affect the accuracy of the scanning process.

title: AI Enabled Automated Digital Image Analysis for Peri-Implant Health Monitoring: A Preliminary Diagnostic Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To develop and validate an AI‐driven Digital Erythema Score (DES) for objective, non‐invasive assessment of peri‐implant mucosal erythema using intraoral scan (IOS) data. Materials and Methods An internal dataset (200 patients, 265 implants) was utilized, with the reference standard established via consensus by two independent experts. We developed a U‐Net model to automatically segment the peri‐implant mucosal margins to calculate the DES and diagnose erythema (modified Gingival Index mGI 0, ≥ 1). We used the YOLO model for object detection to localize erythema regions. The system's diagnostic performance was validated on an independent external dataset (23 patients, 30 implants), supplemented by a multi‐observer study to evaluate the AI's assistance across clinicians with varying experience levels. Results The U‐Net model achieved precise ROI segmentation (Dice similarity coefficient 0.69 ± 0.11) and reliable colorimetric calculation (ICC > 0.95). At the optimal threshold, the DES accurately identified mucosal erythema (AUC, internal 0.9228 [95% CI: 0.8533 to 0.9760], external 0.9018 [0.8135 to 0.9773]). DES and mGI showed significant correlations with bleeding on probing ( B = 7.38, OR = 5.32, both p ). The YOLO model localized inflammatory regions (mAP internal 0.8968, external 0.6820). In the external validation, the DES‐driven diagnostic framework enhanced the diagnostic performance of observers with different levels of experience and increased the inter‐observer consistency. Conclusions The DES provides an objective metric that converts chromatic signals into a diagnostic score and is significantly correlated with clinical inflammation. This AI‐driven framework reduces clinical subjectivity and establishes a non‐invasive paradigm for teledentistry and high‐frequency, home‐based monitoring of peri‐implant health in the future after validation with patient‐accessible imaging devices. Trial Registration This study has been prospectively registered (NCT07349095)

title: Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Outcomes of Radiographically Detected Void Formation Following Lateral Sinus Floor Elevation: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To investigate the prevalence, risk factors, and impact of void formation within graft materials following lateral sinus floor elevation (LSFE) on long‐term implant survival. Materials and Methods This retrospective study analyzed 307 patients who underwent LSFE between 2018 and 2023. Voids were identified on 6‐month postoperative cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT), and patient‐, anatomical‐, and surgery‐related variables were assessed. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression and multivariable logistic regression were used to identify independent risk factors. Implant survival in void versus non‐void groups was compared using Kaplan–Meier analysis and the log‐rank test. Results Voids were detected in 31.3% of cases (96/307). Three independent risk factors were identified: a specific graft material (OR = 4.02, 95% CI: 1.73–9.33, p = 0.001), increased graft amount (OR = 2.20, 95% CI: 1.20–4.01, p = 0.011), and a smaller sinus mucosa tension angle (SMTA; OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.96–1.00, p = 0.027). In a sensitivity analysis confined to conventional graft materials, graft material amount remained robust (OR = 2.02, p = 0.025), with Stage III periodontitis, multiple‐tooth units, and endo‐sinus bone gain additionally identified, whereas membrane perforation was unexpectedly protective (OR = 0.30, p = 0.049). Over a mean 46.6‐month follow‐up, voids were significantly associated with a higher implant failure rate (7.3% vs. 1.9%) and reduced cumulative survival ( p = 0.014). Conclusions Radiographically detected voids following LSFE are associated with increased implant failure and lower cumulative survival. Void formation was independently associated with graft composition, graft material amount, and SMTA; the association with graft material amount persisted after excluding one specific material. Membrane perforation showed an unexpected protective association requiring prospective validation.

title: Treatment of Small Peri‐Implant Buccal Dehiscence Defects With SCTG or GBR : 3‐Year Results of a Pilot Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To evaluate and compare subepithelial connective tissue grafts (SCTG) and guided bone regeneration (GBR) for the treatment of small peri‐implant buccal bone dehiscences over a 3‐year follow‐up, in terms of profilometric contour change, peri‐implant parameters and patient‐reported outcome measures (PROMs). Material and Methods Patients presenting with small buccal bone dehiscences (≤ 3 mm) after single implant placement were included. Defect sites were randomly treated with either SCTG or GBR, while five patients without dehiscences served as a negative control group. All patients received an implant crown and were followed for 3 years. Profilometric measurements, marginal bone levels, peri‐implant parameters, and PROMs were recorded at baseline, 1, and 3 years. Data were analyzed descriptively. Results A total of 16 patients were available for the 3‐year follow‐up (SCTG, n = 5; GBR, n = 6; negative control, n = 5). Both augmentation approaches maintained stable buccal soft‐tissue contours. At 1 mm below the mucosal margin, the median buccal contour change was 0.19 mm (Q1: −0.28; Q3: 0.29) in the SCTG group and 0.11 mm (Q1: −0.20; Q3: 0.30) in the GBR group. At 3 mm below the mucosal margin, the corresponding median contour changes were 0.05 mm (Q1: −0.36; Q3: 0.31) for SCTG and −0.05 mm (Q1: −0.22; Q3: 0.07) for GBR. Peri‐implant clinical parameters (probing depth, bleeding on probing, and plaque) remained stable, indicating maintained peri‐implant health in both groups. Marginal bone levels were preserved throughout the observation period and oral health‐related quality of life remained high and comparable between the SCTG and GBR groups. Conclusion Within the limitations of this pilot study, both SCTG and GBR were associated with stable buccal contour conditions and favorable peri‐implant health over a 3‐year follow‐up period. These findings were observed under adequate self‐performed plaque control and adherence to supportive care. Adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Development and External Validation of An Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Severity Stratification of Current Periodontitis Using Routine Blood Biomarkers, With Exploratory Analyses of Age- and Sex-Specific Model Behaviour.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model using routine laboratory data to distinguish current Stage III–IV from Stage I–II periodontitis among adults with established periodontitis. Materials and Methods This two‐centre retrospective study included 1321 patients for development and 584 for external validation at two hospitals of the Zhejiang University School of Medicine. The stacking model used age, sex, smoking status and 13 blood‐derived predictors and was frozen before external validation. Performance was assessed by discrimination, calibration, classification measures, decision‐curve analysis and comparison with simpler models. SHAP and restricted cubic spline analyses were exploratory. Results The stacking model had an out‐of‐fold AUC of 0.827 (95% CI: 0.802–0.851) in development and an external AUC of 0.774 (95% CI: 0.730–0.818). External calibration was less favourable (intercept 0.785, slope 0.822). External AUC was 0.745 for age, sex and smoking status and 0.763 after adding the 13 blood‐derived predictors. Conclusions Among adults with established periodontitis and sufficiently complete predictor data, the model showed moderate external discrimination but less favourable calibration. Blood‐derived predictors added modest discrimination beyond age, sex and smoking status. The model does not replace periodontal examination. Further multi‐centre validation and calibration are needed before clinical use.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Synthetic and Xenogeneic Self-Retaining Bone Grafting Systems Under Standardized Block Geometry: An Experimental In Vivo Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives This study aimed to compare new bone formation and dimensional outcomes between synthetic and xenogeneic self‐retaining bone grafting systems in staged alveolar ridge augmentation (ARA) for severe bone defects. Methods Eight beagle dogs underwent bilateral extraction of the maxillary premolars, followed by an 8‐week healing period allowing natural alveolar ridge defects. In a split‐mouth design, each animal received both treatments on contralateral sides, with side allocation determined by a computer‐generated randomization sequence: a self‐retaining synthetic bone block (srSB) with particulate synthetic bone (SP), or a self‐retaining xenogeneic block (srXB) with particulate xenogeneic bone (XP), each covered with a collagen membrane. After an additional 8‐week healing period, radiographic and histomorphometric analyses were performed. Results The total augmented area did not differ significantly between groups. However, the amount of newly formed bone was greater in the srSB group than in the srXB group (7.86 ± 1.05 and 4.44 ± 2.33 mm 2 , respectively; mean within‐animal difference 3.38 mm 2 , 95% CI 0.54–6.21, p = 0.028). Linear measurements showed no significant difference in the total augmented buccopalatal width. The horizontal distance to the most buccally located newly formed bone was greater in the srSB group in the mid‐portion of the augmented compartment, reaching significance at 3 mm apical to the alveolar crest after Holm–Bonferroni correction (mean difference 3.57 mm, 95% CI 1.84–5.30, adjusted p = 0.025). Conclusion The synthetic self‐retaining grafting system showed greater new bone formation than the xenogeneic system after 8 weeks of healing in this canine model.

title: Influence of the Occupying Proportion of Mineralised Particles Within the Grafted Volume on Subsequent Volume Shrinkage: A Preclinical Study on Rabbit Calvaria.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To evaluate whether mineral particle occupancy within the grafted volume influences volumetric stability and bone regeneration, and to compare particulate grafts, collagenated grafts, hyaluronic acid–conjugated particulates and mechanical manipulation in a vertical augmentation model. Volumetric stability and mineralised tissue volume were assessed by micro‐computed tomography, and the total augmented area, new bone formation, residual material and particle length were evaluated by histological and histomorphometric analyses. Data were analysed using linear mixed‐effects models. Results Mineralised tissue volume increased over time in Control, CBM and HA groups but decreased in cCBM (time × material interaction, p = 0.020). Reducing graft manipulation may enhance space maintenance and facilitate bone regeneration.

title: One-Year Outcomes of Chairside Fully Guided Versus Conventional Partially Guided Implant Placement With Transcrestal Sinus Augmentation: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives This study represents the 1‐year follow‐up of a previously reported randomized controlled trial comparing chairside fully guided (FG) flapless implant placement with conventional partially guided (PG) open‐flap implant placement. We evaluated marginal bone level (MBL) change, peri‐implant clinical outcomes, and associations between placement accuracy and MBL change. Materials and Methods This study was a 1‐year follow‐up analysis of a previously reported randomized controlled trial. Fifty‐six patients were randomized into the FG ( n = 28) and PG ( n = 28) groups. Radiographic MBL changes and peri‐implant clinical indices were evaluated at baseline and 1‐year post‐loading. Deviations between the virtually planned and placed implants were quantified in three dimensions. Stepwise multiple linear regression analyses were performed to identify accuracy parameters associated with MBL changes. Results Twenty‐one FG and 22 PG patients completed follow‐up. Peri‐implant clinical parameters were comparable between groups. In unadjusted analyses, the FG group showed more positive mesial and mean ΔMBL values than the PG group. However, the treatment group was not significantly associated with mesial, distal, or mean ΔMBL in the adjusted models. Implant accuracy was higher in the FG group, with lower horizontal, three‐dimensional, and angular deviations. Adjusted regression analyses retained TPD and distal EA in the mesial ΔMBL model and VAD in the mean ΔMBL model. Conclusions Chairside, FG flapless implant placement improved positional accuracy and was associated with modest unadjusted differences in short‐term marginal bone level changes after crestal sinus augmentation. However, the between‐group differences in ΔMBL were not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. title: Teriparatide Topical Delivery Supports Osseointegration in Ovariectomized Rats Receiving Cafeteria Diet and Bisphosphonate: An In Vivo Experimental Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Postmenopausal osteoporosis associated with cafeteria diet and bisphosphonate therapy may impair peri‐implant bone repair. Therefore, strategies to enhance osseointegration are needed. Aim This study investigated whether teriparatide‐coated implant surfaces enhance osseointegration in a rodent model of estrogen deficiency (OVX) and cafeteria diet (CD) treated with risedronate (RIS). Material and Methods In the in vitro phase, titanium discs coated with 10 or 40 ng of teriparatide were evaluated by in vitro bioassays, and drug adsorption was confirmed by UV–Vis spectroscopy. As both loading amounts produced similar biological responses, 10 ng was selected for the in vivo phase. In the in vivo phase, 48 rats were randomly assigned to SHAM (sham‐operated control), OVX/CD (ovariectomized with cafeteria diet), or OVX/CD/RIS (ovariectomized with cafeteria diet and risedronate) groups. Titanium implants either coated with teriparatide using a layer‐by‐layer topical drug delivery system or left non‐coated were placed bilaterally in the maxilla. Rats were euthanized after 28 days. Osseointegration was evaluated by removal torque testing, micro computed tomography, fluorescence microscopy, and RT‐qPCR analysis. Results In the cell culture experiment, both teriparatide amounts successfully promoted mineralized nodule formation in vitro and UV–Vis spectroscopy confirmed drug adsorption. In vivo, teriparatide significantly increased removal torque across all groups, with the greatest increase in OVX/CD/RIS. Teriparatide also increased peri‐implant bone volume in OVX/CD and OVX/CD/RIS, confirmed by micro computed tomography and fluorescence microscopy. RT‐qPCR also confirmed upregulation of osteogenic and angiogenic markers. Conclusion Topical teriparatide delivery improves peri‐implant bone repair under estrogen deficiency, cafeteria diet, and bisphosphonate therapy.

title: Diagnosed Dental Diseases, Tooth Loss and the Risk of Primary Liver Cancer in a Nationwide Swedish Cohort.
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aim Poor dental health has been shown to increase the risk of several types of cancer, but its association with primary liver cancer (PLC) remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate the association between dental diseases, tooth loss and the risk of PLC. Patients and Methods We conducted a large population‐based retrospective cohort study including 5,893,325 adults registered in the Swedish Dental Health Register between 2009 and 2016. Participants were linked to multiple Swedish national registers to ascertain incident PLC cases. Cox regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between dental diseases, tooth loss and the risk of PLC, using attained age as the timescale and adjusting for potential confounders. Additionally, in a sibling comparison analysis we controlled for shared genetic and early‐life environmental factors. Results During a mean follow‐up of 6.36 years, 2374 PLC cases were identified through linkage with the Cancer Register: 1856 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and 518 non‐HCC PLC cases. Both caries (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.02–1.30) and periodontitis (HR = 1.25, 95% CI: 1.12–1.39) were associated with an increased risk of PLC. Further, a clear dose–response relationship was observed between fewer remaining teeth and PLC risk, with HRs ranging from 1.15 to 1.84 ( p 27 remaining teeth. Subtype‐specific analyses showed that caries was associated with non‐HCC PLC, whereas periodontitis was associated with HCC. Tooth loss was more strongly associated with HCC than with non‐HCC PLC. The overall findings were generally consistent across sibling‐controlled, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Our large population‐based cohort study suggests that caries, periodontitis and tooth loss are associated with an elevated risk of PLC, with distinct patterns of association observed for HCC and non‐HCC PLC.

title: Factors Associated With Patient-Reported Outcomes More Than 5 Years After Dental Implant Therapy: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To evaluate patient‐reported outcome (PROs) and their associated factors in patients treated with dental implants more than 5 years earlier. Materials and Methods In this cross‐sectional study, patients with implants (> 5 years) completed a self‐administered questionnaire assessing functional, aesthetic, psychosocial and economic satisfaction. The 17 satisfaction items were condensed by exploratory factor analysis, and a Global Satisfaction Score was derived. Univariable and multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors identified factors associated with satisfaction, complemented by sensitivity and subgroup analyses. Results A total of 260 patients were included (61.2% female; 91.5% aged > 50 years). Overall satisfaction was high, with 93.1% of patients satisfied or very satisfied. Factor analysis yielded four dimensions (overall satisfaction, psychosocial function, aesthetics, information). In the multivariable model, higher pre‐treatment information ( β = +6.4, p β = −8.2, p p = 0.030). Conclusions Patient satisfaction more than 5 years after implant therapy was high and most strongly associated with patient‐reported pre‐treatment information and the absence of reported complications than with demographic factors. These findings should be interpreted cautiously as the cross‐sectional design and retrospective self‐reporting preclude causal inference.

title: An Exploratory Longitudinal Analysis of Salivary Host, Bacterial and Fungal Extracellular Vesicles Following 6-Month Non-Surgical Periodontal Therapy in Periodontitis.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To evaluate the longitudinal changes in salivary host and non‐host extracellular vesicles (EVs) following non‐surgical periodontal therapy (NSPT). Materials and Methods Unstimulated saliva and plaque (from a deep pocket) were collected from 25 Stage III/IV periodontitis patients at baseline and at 3 and 6 months post NSPT. Host salivary EVs and non‐host EVs were isolated using immunoaffinity, and size‐exclusion chromatography, respectively. Host EV cytokines were assessed by multiplex flow cytometry, and non‐host EVs, saliva and plaque were profiled by 16S rRNA and fungal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequencing. Results Periodontal parameters significantly decreased at 3 and 6 months post NSPT (vs. baseline), accompanied by increased host‐EVs associated cytokines interleukin‐4 (IL‐4), IL‐12 and IL‐9 (not whole saliva). At both timepoints, bacterial EVs also declined, including the genera Filifactor , Parvimonas and Lentimicrobium and the species Fusobacterium nucleatum , Filifactor alocis , Tannerella forsythia , Treponema denticola , Porphyromonas gingivalis , P. endodontalis , P. micra and Lachnospiraceae bacterium; similar reductions were observed in plaque and saliva taxa, including Treponema , Tannerella , Parvimonas , T. forsythia , T. socranskii and P. micra . At 6 months, fungal EVs from Malassezia arunalokei were decreased and the fungal Candida parapsilosis EVs were increased. Conclusions NSPT led to changes in salivary host and non‐host EV cargoes, suggesting that they may serve as a non‐invasive tool for disease treatment monitoring in periodontitis.

title: Contemporary zygomatic implant rehabilitation: A critical review of the evidence and clinical recommendations
abstract: Abstract Background Zygomatic implant (ZI) therapy has evolved over the past two decades into an established modality for the rehabilitation of the severely atrophic maxilla, avoiding extensive bone augmentation procedures. Aim While the efficacy of ZI therapy is well established, variability in its clinical implementation and remaining knowledge gaps continue to influence its application in clinical practice. Methods This critical review, based on a focused PubMed/MEDLINE search, synthesized higher‐level and long‐term evidence on surgical approaches, loading protocols, indications and outcomes, complications, prosthetic considerations, digital workflows, and current consensus recommendations. Results Current evidence demonstrates favorable long‐term survival across a broad range of ZI indications. The Quad Zygoma Protocol has further expanded graftless rehabilitation for the severely atrophic edentulous maxilla. Surgical approach selection should be guided by maxillozygomatic anatomy and prosthetically driven planning, while digital technologies have progressively shifted ZI surgery toward precision‐oriented workflows. Nevertheless, heterogeneous complication profiles, inconsistent definitions of treatment success, and limited reporting of patient‐reported and long‐term biological and prosthetic outcomes remain important limitations. Conclusions Contemporary ZI rehabilitation represents an established treatment modality for complex maxillary rehabilitation, with the current focus shifting from demonstrating efficacy toward improving treatment predictability and long‐term outcomes. Clinical Recommendations Appropriate case selection is fundamental to successful ZI rehabilitation. Surgical planning should integrate anatomical feasibility, implant emergence, and restorative design, while structured maintenance and patient compliance support long‐term success. Digital workflows can enhance surgical accuracy and reproducibility but require surgical experience and clinical judgment.

title: Combined Host-Derived and Microbiological Biomarkers for the Detection of Peri-Implant Bone Loss: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of host‐derived and microbiological biomarkers, alone and in combination with clinical parameters, for the detection of peri‐implant bone loss (BL). Methods A university‐based cohort of subjects with dental implants was examined at baseline and after a mean follow‐up of 3.9 years. Peri‐implant BL served as the reference standard, defined as > 1 mm between baseline and follow‐up radiographs; implants with Results Seventy‐one subjects with 273 implants were included. Twenty‐eight exhibited peri‐implant‐BL > 1.0 mm over the follow‐up period. Increased levels of IL‐1β, T. denticola, Fusobacterium spp., and T. forsythia were associated with BL in unadjusted analyses. However, these associations were no longer statistically significant after adjustment for clinical parameters. Individual biomarkers demonstrated limited diagnostic accuracy (maximum AUC = 0.68). In contrast, biomarker combinations with clinical parameters exhibited excellent discriminative performance (AUC > 0.95). The combination of IL‐1β and BoP‐or‐PPD achieved the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.97). Conclusions While individual biomarkers showed limited diagnostic utility, combining multiple predictors significantly improved the ability to detect peri‐implant BL. Combining IL‐1β with either BoP or PPD significantly outperformed individual clinical measures but did not outperform the combination of clinical parameters, highlighting the potential of integrated biomarker and clinical parameter approaches as screening tools for detecting BL.

title: Premature Occlusal Contacts Induce MRONJ in Osseointegrated Dental Implants: An Experimental In Vivo Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives Medication‐related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a debilitating condition associated with antiresorptive agents (ARAs) and can occur around well‐osseointegrated dental implants. Although implant presence–triggered osteonecrosis (IPTO) has been primarily linked to bacteria‐related peri‐implantitis, whether occlusal trauma contributes to IPTO remains unclear. Therefore, this study developed a novel premature occlusal contact (POC) mouse implant model to evaluate the effect of occlusal trauma on MRONJ development around osseointegrated implants. Material and Methods Eighteen mice underwent bilateral maxillary first molar extraction followed by immediate implant placement. After a 3‐week healing period to allow osseointegration, mice were randomized to receive intravenous zoledronic acid (ZOL, 125 μg/kg) or saline vehicle (Veh) twice weekly ( n = 9 per group). One week later, POC was induced in a split‐mouth design by applying composite resin to one implant, whereas the contralateral implant served as a control. After 5 weeks of occlusal loading, mice were euthanized for μCT and histological analyses. Results μCT analysis revealed that POC reduced radiographic bone‐to‐implant contact (rBIC) in both Veh‐ and ZOL‐treated mice. POC significantly increased empty lacunae around the implant neck in Veh‐treated mice, whereas in ZOL‐treated mice, POC induced extensive circumferential bone necrosis around the implant, accompanied by increased macrophage infiltration. No significant differences in peptidoglycan (PGN)‐positive signals were observed among the experimental groups. Conclusion These findings suggest that POC contributes to peri‐implant osteonecrosis under ZOL treatment, supporting occlusal trauma as an important local factor in MRONJ development around osseointegrated dental implants.

title: Masseter Muscle Volume and Cross‐Sectional Area as Risk Factors for Late Mechanical Dental Implant Failure: A Matched Case–Control Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives This study aimed to investigate whether three‐dimensional (3D) masseter muscle morphology—volume and cross‐sectional area (CSA)—is associated with the risk of late mechanical dental implant failure and to derive preliminary cut‐off values for risk stratification. Material and Methods This 1:4 matched case–control study investigated 23 cases of late mechanical failure (fixture fracture, screw fracture, or abutment fracture) and 92 successful controls. Participants were matched by gender, age (±10 years), anatomical location, and maintenance period (±2 years). Masseter morphology was quantified using the 3D reconstruction of the cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) data. Independent risk factors were determined using a multivariable generalized estimating equation model adjusting for potential confounders. Results Increased masseter muscle bulk was significantly associated with mechanical failure ( p 3 increase in masseter volume and by 1.11‐fold per 10 mm 2 increase in CSA. ROC analysis demonstrated AUCs of 0.846 for masseter volume and 0.871 for CSA. The maximum‐Youden thresholds were 31,272.56 mm 3 for volume and 691.30 mm 2 for CSA, with sensitivities of 86.96% and 82.61% and specificities of 77.17% and 79.35%, respectively. Internal bootstrap validation yielded AUC 95% confidence intervals of 0.751–0.931 and 0.767–0.951, respectively. Conclusions Greater masseter muscle volume and CSA were significantly associated with late mechanical implant failure in this matched case–control study. The proposed cut‐off values may provide preliminary reference values for risk stratification. However, these findings should be regarded as exploratory and require prospective validation in independent cohorts before routine clinical implementation.

title: Intraoral Ultrasonography for Mid-Buccal Probing Depth Assessment: A Proof-of-Concept Clinical Agreement Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To evaluate the agreement between ultrasound‐derived gingival sulcus depth ( uGSD ) and clinical probing depth ( PD ) at standardised mid‐buccal sites as a proof‐of‐concept study. Materials and Methods Mid‐buccal measurements were obtained from 963 sites in 69 participants (767 anterior, 127 premolars, 69 first molars) using an 18‐MHz ultrasound transducer and a UNC‐15 probe. uGSD was measured on B‐mode images; reliability was assessed by two trained examiners. Agreement was evaluated using intra‐class correlation coefficient (ICC), Bland–Altman analysis and mean absolute error (MAE). Generalised estimating equations and clustered ICCs accounted for within‐patient clustering. Subgroups included PD strata, bleeding, tooth type, calculus, restorations (prosthetic crowns/orthodontic attachments) and smoking. Results Ultrasound measurements showed high reliability (ICCs > 0.90). Agreement between uGSD and clinical PD was strong (ICC = 0.942; 95% CI: 0.935–0.949), with negligible mean difference (+0.023 mm) and low MAE (0.29 ± 0.32 mm). Subgroup ICCs ranged from 0.786 to 0.952; 85.0% of sites differed by ≤ 0.50 mm and 96.7% by ≤ 1.00 mm. Molar sites showed the highest MAE (0.38 mm) and slight underestimation (−0.123 mm). Conclusion Intraoral ultrasonography showed high agreement with clinical PD at standardised mid‐buccal sites in anterior teeth, premolars and first molars. It may serve as a non‐invasive adjunct to conventional probing; however, broader studies are needed across complex sites and examiner experience levels.
